summary: A passage from a novel in which Rebecca, a young soap seller, chats with a well-dressed gentleman on a porch while trying to sell him Rose-Red and Snow-White soap. The customer already knows the soap's virtues, and their talk turns to childhood hardships, with Rebecca admitting her childhood had no shoes, too many babies and not enough books. The man, who is only visiting his aunt's house, reveals his own unhappy childhood of hunger and want, and Rebecca wonders whether he is truly happy. The excerpt ends with Rebecca explaining that she and her silent partner, who is holding the horse at the gate, are not selling for their own benefit.
one_line: Rebecca, a young soap seller, chats with a gentleman customer on a porch about soap, childhood hardships and happiness.
key_facts: Rebecca offers the gentleman a soap described as the best now on the market.
The gentleman says he must know that soap and asks whether it is made out of pure vegetable fats.
Rebecca says the soap has no acid in it and that a child could do the Monday washing with it using no force.
The ornamental box holds the Rose-Red soap, and the prices of both the Rose-Red and the Snow-White soaps are unfolded.
The gentleman says he is keeping house but does not live there, and is only on a visit to his aunt, who has gone to Portland.
The gentleman says he used to be at the farm as a boy and is very fond of the spot.
Rebecca observes that nothing takes the place of the farm where one lived as a child.
The gentleman says his own childhood was a particularly unpleasant one.
Rebecca says her worst childhood trouble was no shoes and too many babies and not enough books.
The gentleman says his worst trouble was lack of food and clothes principally.
Rebecca notices that the gentleman's eyes were tired and his mouth sad when he was not speaking, despite his prosperous look.
The gentleman asks how much soap he ought to buy, and Rebecca suggests he consider how much his aunt has on hand.
Rebecca says she will look in the circular to see whether soap keeps.
Rebecca says they are not selling for their own benefit, and her friend is holding the horse at the gate.
